name: Emeka Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on my father-in-law's place, Kingsmead, off the Church Road. Harold's seventy and he's farmed it fifty years: wheat, barley, about eighty beef cattle and a flock of ewes. I came three years ago after eighteen years on the bottling line at the brewery in town. My day is feeding cattle at seven, checking the sheep, then whatever Harold has written on the board in the kitchen. He still writes it in chalk.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like working next to Harold. He doesn't say much, but when he does, it's worth hearing. I like that it's family land and my boy might farm it one day. What wears me out is how much I don't know. I still can't judge when the barley's ready. Harold bites a grain and knows. I bite one and just get a mouthful of barley.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, good, let the computer people get on with their computers and leave the farming to farmers. I'd say that after church, probably, to the men who ask how the cattle are doing. I don't go on the internet for opinions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd thank God. I've got maybe ten years to learn this farm from Harold, and I need every one of them. I don't want anything changing the rules while I'm still learning them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going. Learn the barley. Help Harold with the lambing in March. We'd keep putting money away like Grace and I always have, a bit each month, and keep the farm accounts the way Harold does, in the green book.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like Sunday afternoon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said ten years to learn the farm from Harold. What happens after?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's told Grace the farm comes to her, and she wants me to run it. So it's my job to be ready. If I'm not, we'd have to rent the land to the big outfit next door. Harold would rather die than see that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of AI you'd use, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Grace uses something on her phone to write the parish newsletter, and that's her business. I've never used it and I don't need to. A cow doesn't care what my phone thinks.

S0.say: I'd say good, let the computer people keep their computers and leave farming to farmers. I'd say it after church to the men who ask about the cattle.
S0.think: Honestly I'd thank God, because I need about ten years to learn Kingsmead from Harold. I don't want the rules changing while I'm still learning them.
S0.do: Keeps learning the barley and helping Harold with March lambing, and goes on saving a bit each month. Keeps the farm accounts in Harold's green book as before.
S0.quote: I've never used it and I don't need to. A cow doesn't care what my phone thinks.
S0.fieldNote: Emeka sees himself as the heir-in-training to his father-in-law's farm, and his whole plan depends on time to learn. Faith and family come through in nearly every answer. He's clear and unbothered about never using AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farms have always changed, and good farmers change slowly. I'd say Harold's generation went from small fields to big ones without anyone holding their hand. We'll manage. I wouldn't want the government paying people to sit at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be worried about the neighbours, not about us. The big outfit next door, the Crawleys, would buy every robot going and farm cheaper than us. We're a family place. We'd lose on price, slowly, every year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, nothing much. Keep going, keep learning. I'd talk to Harold about whether we keep the sheep, because they're the most work and the first thing a big farm would undercut us on. I'd not buy any robots. Maybe we'd put a bit more aside each month, to be safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like weather coming in from the west. Not here yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't want the government paying people to sit at home. What would you want instead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Apprenticeships. Proper ones, a young lad next to an old farmer. That's how Harold learned and how I'm learning. If jobs change, teach people the new jobs by working, not with a cheque.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Harold, a bit. He'd see the Crawleys with their robots and feel old. And Joe, the lad from the village who helps at harvest. He's nineteen, he's got nothing else lined up.

S1.say: I'd say farms have always changed and good farmers change slowly, and that we'll manage like Harold's generation did. I wouldn't want government paying people to sit at home.
S1.think: I'd worry about the big farm next door buying every robot and farming cheaper than us. As a family place we'd lose on price, slowly, every year.
S1.do: Keeps going and learning in the first year, and talks with Harold about dropping the sheep. Buys no robots and puts a little more aside each month.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like weather building in the west.
S1.quote: We're a family place. We'd lose on price, slowly, every year.
S1.fieldNote: His worry isn't losing his own job but the family farm being undercut by a bigger, automated neighbour. He favours apprenticeships over welfare, in line with his traditional views. He worries for his father-in-law's pride and a young harvest helper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tech companies have gone too far, and the politicians in the cities let them because they've never set foot on a farm. I'd say it after church and I'd say it in the polling booth. That's where I do my talking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. I'd be the man who gave up a steady job to learn a farm just as farms stopped needing men. That's what I'd think, lying in bed. We'd be all right for money, we've the house and savings and Grace's family has the land. But land with nothing to do on it is just a view.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Harold and Grace the first week and talk it through properly, as a family. I'd cut spending, the new pickup can wait. I'd keep farming the old way as long as anyone will buy what we grow, because I'm not learning robots at forty-three. I'd lean on the church too, because people will be frightened and we'll need each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, if I'm honest. And angry. I'd pray about it, which helps a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said land with nothing to do on it is just a view. What would you tell Daniel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Daniel's twelve and he already thinks he's a farmer. I'd tell him the land is ours whatever happens, and we look after it. I don't know what else I'd tell him. That's the part that keeps me awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're angry. Angry at whom?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the people who built it in a hurry to get rich. And a bit at myself, for leaving the brewery late. If I'd come to the farm at twenty-five, I'd at least have known it properly before it went.

S2.say: I'd say the tech companies have gone too far, and city politicians who've never set foot on a farm let them. I'd say it after church and at the polling booth.
S2.think: I'd be the man who gave up a steady job to learn a farm just as farms stopped needing men. We'd be all right for money, but land with nothing to do on it is just a view.
S2.do: Holds a family meeting with Harold and Grace in the first week and puts off buying a new pickup. Keeps farming the old way without robots and leans on his church community.
S2.feel: Scared and angry, finding some comfort in prayer.
S2.quote: But land with nothing to do on it is just a view.
S2.fieldNote: Money isn't the threat for him; purpose and his family's way of life are. He blames tech companies and city politicians, and also himself for coming to farming late. Church and family are his first places to turn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as the fast one, but I'd say we've got five years, so the farming groups should be making a noise now. Protect the family farms. I'd say that and vote that way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, Harold's seventy-five and maybe stepping back. I'd be running Kingsmead just as the robots arrive. I'd have to decide whether to buy them or sell to the Crawleys. I don't want either. That's the honest truth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first year learning everything Harold knows, faster, every evening if he'll sit with me. I'd put more by each month, maybe four hundred, so we could hold on through a couple of bad years. And I'd ask at church whether other families would share kit or labour, the way farms used to at harvest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. But I'd have time to pray on it and plan, which matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask other families to share. Has that worked before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Harold remembers when five farms round here shared one combine and helped each other at harvest. It stopped in the eighties. Maybe it comes back. Families helping families is better than a robot from a company in another country.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If buying a robot meant keeping the farm, would you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hate it. Maybe, if Grace and Harold said so. I'd want someone else to run it. I'd be the one with the cattle, the old way, for as long as they'd let me.

S3.say: I'd say five years means the farming groups should be making a noise now to protect family farms, and I'd vote that way.
S3.think: In five years I'd be running Kingsmead just as robots arrive, and I'd have to choose between buying them or selling to the Crawleys. Honestly, I don't want either.
S3.do: Spends the first year learning everything he can from Harold, every evening if possible. Saves about four hundred a month extra and asks church families about sharing equipment and labour as farms used to.
S3.feel: Anxious, but grateful for time to pray and plan.
S3.quote: Families helping families is better than a robot from a company in another country.
S3.fieldNote: The extra years give him time to plan, and his plan looks backwards to farms sharing machines and labour. He faces an inheritance decision he dislikes either way. Even when pressed, he'd only accept a robot if the family decided and someone else ran it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for families to plan, so plan. Don't wait for government. I'd say it to the men at church, and to my boy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'm fifty-three, Harold's likely gone, and Kingsmead is mine and Grace's to run. I'd have had time to learn it. Then the robots come and I'm an old dog with old tricks. But I'd be an old dog on his own land, and that's more than most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, mostly. Learn the farm. Keep saving. I'd talk to Daniel about doing an agricultural apprenticeship when he leaves school, so he learns the new machines properly and I don't have to. That's how a family covers itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not frightened. Ten years is a long time in farming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Daniel learns the machines so you don't have to. Is that fair on him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not. Grace said the same thing. But every generation does a bit of what the last couldn't. Harold did the tractors, I'd do the land, Daniel does the robots. That's how I'd see it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the money side over ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pay off the house first. Then keep money aside for Ruth, our girl, whatever she wants to do. I'd not put it in shares or anything I don't understand.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough for families to plan, so they should plan and not wait for government. I'd say it at church and to my son.
S4.think: At fifty-three I'd have had time to learn the farm, and then the robots come and I'm an old dog with old tricks. But I'd be an old dog on my own land, which is more than most.
S4.do: Keeps farming and saving, and pays off the house first. Talks with his son Daniel about an agricultural apprenticeship after school so the next generation learns the machines.
S4.quote: Harold did the tractors, I'd do the land, Daniel does the robots.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years settles him, because the farm becomes his to run before the end point. He'd hand the learning of the new machines to his son, and admits that may not be fair. He keeps money away from anything he doesn't understand.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. We'd have the land and the savings, but no time for me to learn it or for families to sort themselves out. What would help is proper apprenticeships, paid, on real farms, and some protection for family farms against the big outfits that can buy all the robots at once.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. People think it's old-fashioned. But if the work goes, what's left is family, church and land. I'd rather have those three than a cheque from the government.

headlineQuote: Harold bites a grain and knows. I bite one and just get a mouthful of barley.
portrait: Emeka Silva is 43, a former brewery bottling-line worker learning to farm on his father-in-law Harold's wheat, beef and sheep farm, which his wife is due to inherit. He's a churchgoer who prefers apprenticeships to handouts, never uses AI and has no plans to start. His fear isn't about money, since the family has savings and land, but about the farm being undercut by a bigger automated neighbour and losing its purpose. The two-year AGI scenario leaves him scared and angry; with five or ten years he plans to learn from Harold, share labour with church families, and leave the robots to his son.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because there would be no time for him to learn the farm or for families to organise themselves.
whatWouldHelp: Paid apprenticeships on real farms, and protection for family farms against big operations that can buy all the robots at once.
